Leonard Bloomfield. An American linguist whose rigorous methodological approach to language description and influential textbook Language, published in nineteen thirty-three, made structural and descriptive linguistics the dominant paradigm in mid-twentieth-century American linguistics. He elevated linguistics from a philological appendage of classical studies into an autonomous empirical science. He authored Language as a comprehensive textbook defining how linguists should approach the systematic, observable study of language, emphasising data over speculation. Bloomfield pioneered structural linguistics in America, treating language as a closed system of elements and their arrangements rather than as a window onto history or psychology. He developed rigorous methods for phonetic transcription, morphological analysis, and dialect mapping, establishing field linguistics as a technical discipline with exacting standards. He studied Native American languages, particularly Menomini and other Algonquian languages, using meticulous descriptive techniques that set new standards for language documentation. His behaviourist approach—holding that meaning arises from use and context, not inner mental states—dominated American linguistics from the nineteen thirties through the nineteen fifties, though it would later be challenged by Noam Chomsky's cognitive revolution.
